what: Kafka is a durable, append-only event log split into topics and partitions. Producers write events once, and many consumer groups read them at their own pace, even replaying old ones.
like: Like a ship's logbook copied onto several ships: entries are only ever added at the end, and every reader keeps a bookmark of the last line they read.
why: Very high throughput by spreading a topic over many partitions and brokers
Events stay for days (or forever), so new readers can replay history
One stream feeds many independent consumer groups without them slowing each other

steps.d: A record with a key is hashed (murmur2) and taken modulo the partition count, so the same key, like user:42, always lands in the same partition.
The partition leader adds the record to the end of its log and gives it the next offset (a position number). Order is kept inside a partition, not across partitions.
Followers copy the leader. With acks=all the leader confirms only once every in-sync replica (ISR) has the record, and min.insync.replicas sets how many must be there.
Each partition is read by exactly one consumer in a group, so a group scales up to one consumer per partition. Other groups read the same data separately.
Consumers commit the next offset they will read into the internal __consumer_offsets topic. After a restart they carry on from that bookmark, or rewind to replay.
KRaft controllers, a Raft quorum, hold cluster metadata and pick new leaders. Old log segments are deleted after the retention time, or compacted to the latest value per key.

numbers.l: default topic retention on Confluent Cloud (retention.ms 604,800,000)
default replication factor on Confluent Cloud: three copies of each partition
default min.insync.replicas on Confluent Cloud, so one replica can fail
release where acks=all and the idempotent producer became defaults
first release running entirely without ZooKeeper (March 2025)

choices.d: Sets the most consumers a group can use in parallel. Pick enough for future load up front, because adding partitions later moves keys and can break per-key ordering.
Use the thing that needs ordering, like order ID or user ID. A key with too much traffic overloads one partition; no key spreads records evenly.
Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2 and acks=all is the usual safe setup. acks=1 is quicker but can lose writes if a leader fails.
Time or size based delete for event streams. cleanup.policy=compact keeps the latest value per key, handy for a changelog or current state.
At-least-once is the default, so make consumers idempotent. For exactly-once, use transactions with read_committed consumers and commit offsets inside the transaction.

instead.why: Simple job queue: each task done once, no replay or partitions to plan
Push fan-out to many subscribers without keeping a long history
Redis Streams for small, short-lived streams you already run Redis for
Cheap long-term archive of events once real-time reading is done

breaks.d: Consumers read slower than producers write, so they fall behind.
breaks.see: Consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) rising per partition
breaks.fix: Add consumers up to the partition count, speed up processing, or add partitions

breaks.d: One key carries most of the traffic, so one partition and broker do most of the work.
breaks.see: One partition with far more bytes in and lag than the rest
breaks.fix: A better key, or add a suffix to spread one hot key over several partitions

breaks.d: Consumers joining or leaving make the group reshuffle partitions, and reading pauses meanwhile.
breaks.see: Frequent rebalance logs and lag spikes when pods restart
breaks.fix: Opt in to the newer consumer group protocol (KIP-848) and keep each batch of work short

breaks.d: A consumer processes records but crashes before committing, so they are read again.
breaks.see: Same event handled twice, e.g. a double email
breaks.fix: Idempotent handlers with an event ID, or transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka flows

breaks.d: Too few in-sync replicas are left for acks=all writes.
breaks.see: Producer errors on acks=all writes while the ISR list has shrunk
breaks.fix: Bring brokers back, spread replicas across zones, alert when the ISR shrinks

say: I'll publish order events to a Kafka topic keyed by order ID, so all events for one order stay in order inside one partition.
I'll start with enough partitions for peak load, because a consumer group can run at most one consumer per partition.
For durability: replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 2 and acks=all, so we can lose a broker without losing acknowledged writes.
Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers are idempotent using the event ID, and new services can replay the topic from the start.

followups.a: Only within a partition. Records with the same key go to the same partition, so per-key order holds. If you need global order you need one partition, which caps throughput.

followups.q: What happens when a broker dies?
followups.a: For each partition it led, the controller picks a new leader from the in-sync replicas. With f+1 replicas Kafka can lose f of them without losing committed records.

The idempotent producer removes duplicate writes using a producer ID and sequence numbers. Transactions write outputs and consumer offsets together, and read_committed consumers only see committed data.

followups.q: Kafka or a plain queue like SQS?
followups.a: Kafka when you need replay, many independent readers, high throughput or per-key order. A queue when each job just needs doing once, with per-message retries and less to run.

today: Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) dropped ZooKeeper completely and runs only in KRaft mode, and it added share groups (KIP-932) in early access for queue-style reading of a topic.

check.q: A topic has 6 partitions. How many consumers in one group can read at the same time?
check.why: Each partition goes to exactly one consumer in a group, so extra consumers sit idle.

check.q: You need all events for one customer handled in order. What do you do?
check.a: Use the customer ID as the record key
d: Use a single consumer group per customer
check.why: Same key, same partition, and order is kept inside a partition.

check.q: With acks=all, when does the leader confirm a write?
check.a: When every in-sync replica has it
d: As soon as the leader writes it
When it is flushed to S3
check.why: acks=all waits for the in-sync replicas, and min.insync.replicas sets the minimum count.

check.q: What does Kafka 4.0 use instead of ZooKeeper?
check.why: A Raft quorum of controllers inside Kafka keeps the cluster metadata.
